annotations.annotation_text: Page 185 opens Book 1, Chapter 7 ("Shem the Penman") during the Age of Gods phase. This passage continues Joyce's devastating self-portrait as Shem the forger-artist who writes on his own skin with bodily secretions, featuring Shem, Shaun (as Justius), ALP (Mercius). The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

annotations.target_phrase: ink from his own bodily secretions
annotations.annotation_text: The famous passage where Shem creates his own ink from excrement, symbolizing the artist transforming the basest aspects of life into literature.
Using lowest materials to create high art; it represents the ultimate artistic alchemy, turning the refuse of history into the golden text of the Wake.
The artist must entirely consume and transform his physical, personal reality to generate his work, making the book a literal extension of his body.
Shem's dwelling place is a 'Haunted Inkbottle' filled with refuse, discarded drafts, and excrement—a direct metaphor for the text of Finnegans Wake itself.
The accumulation of garbage in Shem's house mirrors Joyce's technique of collecting linguistic scraps, gossip, and historical detritus to build his epic.
The concluding trial of the chapter pits Justius (representing the condemnatory Shaun) against Mercius (representing the merciful ALP and Shem's redemption).
The legal interrogation structurally anticipates the later inquest of Yawn, with Shem constantly forced to defend his existence and art.
ALP/Mercius's final words extend forgiveness to Shem, showing that maternal love and understanding transcend fraternal judgment and societal condemnation.

Mid-page polysemic node on page 185 ("Shem the Penman"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Gods dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
